subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Suraj had promised the client the demo on Friday at ten, and the demo needed the data Sunaina had said would arrive on Thursday. On Thursday afternoon her message came: “Almost there, tomorrow morning for sure.” Suraj felt his stomach sink. He called the client to ask for a later slot, moved two colleagues off other work to build a stand-in dataset overnight, and cancelled his own dinner plan. The real data came on Saturday. On Monday Suraj wrote Sunaina's next promised date on the team board with a small question mark beside it, and added two days in his own private notes. “It's not that it slipped,” he told his partner. “It's that I can't rely on her dates now.”

qa.q: What did Suraj do when Sunaina said the data would come tomorrow morning?
qa.a: Suraj called the client for a later slot, moved two colleagues to build a stand-in dataset overnight and cancelled his dinner plan.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when Sunaina's message came?
qa.a: Suraj's stomach sank: he felt alarmed and let down because the demo depended on the data.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do differently when giving her next date?
qa.a: Give an honest, longer estimate with a warning as soon as the date looks unsafe, so Suraj can plan around it.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's colleagues feel about the overnight work?
qa.a: The two colleagues moved off their own work probably feel tired and annoyed at the sudden reshuffle, and may also start doubting Sunaina's dates.

grounding: A person relies on another's promised date and has to reshuffle everything when it slips, and trust erodes.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Salma checked the shared sheet for the third time that week. The vendor onboarding was Kishore's job, and Kishore's date had been “Monday”, then “Wednesday”, then “definitely Friday”. Each promise sounded cheerful, and each time Salma had booked the training room and told the finance team to expect the vendor's account. Each time she had rebooked. This Friday the room was booked again, and again the message came at 5 pm: “Some paperwork pending, sorry!” Salma read it twice, closed the laptop and sat silently for a moment. Then she wrote in the sheet next to Kishore's name a line she would never have added before: “Ask for a real date and what could go wrong.”

qa.q: What dates did Kishore give for the vendor onboarding?
What does Salma feel as she reads the message twice and sits quietly?
qa.a: Salma feels frustrated and let down, and her trust in Kishore's dates is wearing thin.

qa.q: What could Kishore do so the next date is believable?
qa.a: Look at how long onboarding really took before, give a longer honest date, and say early if any paperwork could delay it.

qa.q: How might the finance team feel about waiting for the account?
qa.a: The finance team may be confused and irritated after being told to expect the vendor account three times, which would cost them trust in the plan.

grounding: Repeated optimistic dates force a coordinator to rebook and reshuffle, and trust wears away.
